title: Acme Upgrade Assistant: upgrades that wait for your yes
subtitle: Sample talk track · leadership briefing · 6-minute opening slot, then discussion · target 4:30 of speaking, hard cap 5:30 · fictional product and figures

cue_card.message: The assistant does the how of an upgrade, and nothing changes until a person on your team says yes.

anchors.label: The gap.
anchors.text: The notice gives what and when. 5.5 hours of hands-on time per upgrade is the how.

anchors.label: The gate.
anchors.text: Seven steps, one approval. Nothing changes before it.

anchors.label: The proof.
anchors.text: 42 upgrades, 40 minutes median, 42 of 42 approved by a person.

anchors.label: The ask.
anchors.text: Two teams, eight weeks, one executive sponsor.

cue_card.ask: Two teams for eight weeks, with one executive sponsor. Then the question: which two teams would you put in first?
cue_card.reminders: Off slide 2 by 1:15 · into the ask by 3:30 · say 'target' and 'pilot', never 'guaranteed' · no prices

segments.title: 1 · The whole idea in twenty seconds
segments.purpose: Give a cold room the whole idea before any detail, and set the promise the rest of the talk keeps.
segments.warmth: Name the work the room already carries before naming the product.
segments.competence: One plain sentence with no adjectives: what it does and where the human stays in control.

script.text: "Thanks for the time. Everyone here has an upgrade on their list right now." [pause]
"Here is the whole idea in one line. [slow] **The assistant does the work of an upgrade, and nothing changes until one of your people says yes.**"

segments.transition: "Let me start with why that matters."

segments.title: 2 · The gap: what and when, but not how
segments.purpose: Make the problem concrete with one number the room can repeat.
segments.warmth: Credit the three teams that logged their upgrades by hand; it was their idea.
segments.competence: Say the sample size with the median, and call it a baseline, not an estimate for the whole company.

script.text: [click: the notice] "Every notice tells you two things: what is going out of support, and when."
[click: the list] "It doesn't tell you how. Finding every cluster, reading the release notes, planning the order, testing, running, checking. That part is ours."
[click: the number] "Three of our teams logged twenty upgrades by hand. [pause: let the number land] **The median was 5.5 hours of hands-on time, per upgrade.**"

script.proposal: If you have a short true story about one of those twenty upgrades, tell it here in two sentences. Do not invent one.
script.label: Optional story, your call

segments.transition: "So what would it take to give those hours back without giving up control?"
notes: The 5.5 hours is a baseline from twenty logged upgrades. If someone asks for a company-wide number, say we don't have one yet.

segments.title: 3 · How it works: seven steps, one gate
segments.purpose: Walk the seven steps and make the approval gate the moment they recall.
segments.warmth: Slow down at Approve and look at the leaders; this is the part that protects their teams.
segments.competence: Say which steps are read-only. Precision about what touches production earns the trust.

script.text: [click: Discover] "It starts by finding every cluster the notice covers. [click: Analyze] Then it checks versions and the breaking changes that apply to us."
[click: Plan] "It writes a plan file: the order, the windows, the rollback. [click: Dry run] And it rehearses that plan on a copy."
"Four steps in, it has changed nothing. Everything so far is read-only."
[click: Approve] [pause] [slow: eyes on the room] **"Then it stops. A named person on your team reads the plan and says yes. Until then, nothing changes."**
[click: Execute] "After the yes, it runs the plan in your own pipeline, one window at a time. [click: Validate] And it checks health after each change, and rolls back if a check fails."

segments.transition: "That's the design. Here's what happened in the pilot."

segments.title: 4 · The pilot: hours to minutes
segments.purpose: Prove the design with pilot results, and show the safety net working, not just the speed.
segments.warmth: Present the rollbacks as good news for the people on call, not as a footnote.
segments.competence: Every tile has a source line in the figures file; say 'pilot' so nobody hears a promise.

script.text: [click: 42] "Three teams, six weeks, forty-two database upgrades."
[click: 40 min] "The median hands-on time went from 5.5 hours to **forty minutes**." [pause]
[click: 42 of 42] "Every one of the forty-two had a named approver before anything ran."
[click: 2] [soft: this is the reassuring part] "And two upgrades failed their checks. The assistant stopped and rolled them back on its own. That's the part I'd want if I were on call."

segments.transition: "So what does that change for the teams day to day?"
notes: Fictional sample data. In a real deck every tile must match a line in the figures file.

segments.title: 5 · What changes for your teams
segments.purpose: Translate the mechanics into the teams' week, and land that they keep control.
segments.warmth: Speak about the teams' time, not the tool's features.
segments.competence: Keep each row to one concrete change you can show in the pilot.

script.text: [click] "Today someone reads every release note. Tomorrow they review a plan."
[click] "Today upgrades wait for a free week. Tomorrow they run in the pipeline, one window at a time."
[click] "And every change has a name on it. [slow] **Your pipeline, your approval, your record.**"

segments.title: 6 · What's next, the ask, thank you
segments.purpose: Tie the ask to work that is already scheduled, make it small enough to say yes to today, then open the room.
segments.warmth: Step toward the room for the ask; it is a request, not a pitch.
segments.competence: Name the size of the ask exactly. A small, precise ask is easier to approve than a vague big one.

script.text: [click: 118] "118 clusters reach end of support in the next six months. That work is coming either way."
[click: the ask] [move: toward the room] [pause] "So here is what I'm asking for. **Two teams, eight weeks, and one executive sponsor.**"
[click: the question] "Thank you. [slow: open question] **Which two teams would you put in first?**" [pause: then stop and let them answer]

segments.transition: Hold the silence. Let the room answer first.

questions.q: What if the plan is wrong?
questions.a: "Then nobody approves it. The plan is a file your team reads before anything runs, and the dry run shows what would happen on a copy."

questions.q: Does it need access to production?
questions.a: "Five of the seven steps are read-only. It only changes things in Execute, after the approval, and through your pipeline."
"The ask today is two teams' time for eight weeks and a sponsor. I'll bring a cost estimate to the sponsor in week one."

questions.q: Is 40 minutes what we'd see everywhere?
questions.a: "It's the pilot median across forty-two upgrades. The next phase is how we find out for the rest of the fleet."

timing.note: If the slot shrinks to three minutes, cut slide 5 to its last line and drop the optional story on slide 2; keep the gate line and the ask word for word.

rehearsal: **The 60-second version.** Say slide 1's anchor, the 5.5 hours, the gate line, the 40 minutes and the ask, nothing else. A colleague should be able to repeat the message and the ask.
**Gate line cold (3 times).** Slide 3's Approve paragraph out loud. Listen for a real stop before 'Then it stops' and a slower pace after it.
**Hardest question cold.** Have someone ask 'What will it cost?' without warning. Good sounds like the ⚠ answer in under 15 seconds, with no number you can't source.
**Learn mode pass.** Switch the page to Learn and say each segment from the anchor lines only; click a blurred line to check yourself.
